reference.source: Oral medicine and dermatology reference texts
clinicalPearls: A benign condition in which elongated, poorly desquamated filiform papillae give the dorsum of the tongue a matted, hair-like appearance
The colour ranges from brown to black depending on pigment-producing organisms, foods, tobacco and staining substances
The colour comes from trapped debris and chromogenic micro-organisms rather than from true pigmentation
It is usually asymptomatic but can cause a gagging sensation, halitosis or altered taste
Risk factors include poor oral hygiene, smoking, a soft diet, xerostomia and certain medications and mouthwashes
Management centres on tongue debridement, improved oral hygiene and removing precipitating factors
reference.pathophysiology: Black hairy tongue arises from defective desquamation and consequent hypertrophy and elongation of the filiform papillae on the tongue dorsum. The elongated papillae trap keratin, food debris and micro-organisms, and chromogenic bacteria and yeasts together with exogenous stains produce the characteristic discoloration. Predisposing factors that reduce mechanical cleansing of the tongue, such as a soft diet, dry mouth, smoking and poor hygiene, promote the papillary overgrowth; microbial colonisation contributes to colour but is not a primary infection.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-black hairy tongue from bismuth or food staining
Melanotic or other pigmented mucosal lesions
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic appearance
Medication and habit history (tobacco, mouthwashes, antibiotics)
Assessment of oral hygiene and salivary flow
Biopsy only if an alternative pigmented or keratotic lesion is suspected
redFlags: Persistent lesion despite hygiene measures suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Associated immunosuppression raising concern for oral hairy leukoplakia
reference.prognosis: The condition is entirely benign and reversible, resolving with debridement, better oral hygiene and correction of precipitating factors.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for oral hairy leukoplakia or a pigmented neoplasm
Failing to address smoking and dry mouth
Investigating a clearly benign appearance excessively
management: Regular mechanical debridement of the tongue dorsum by brushing or scraping to remove the elongated, keratin-laden filiform papillae
Improve oral hygiene and increase dietary roughage to promote normal desquamation of the papillae
Remove precipitating factors — smoking cessation, review of offending medications and oxidising mouthwashes, and treatment of xerostomia
Reassure the patient that the condition is entirely benign and reversible
Reserve biopsy for cases where an alternative pigmented or keratotic lesion is suspected
